  39. Worth the detour · Tempura, Tonkatsu & Agemono · Kita & Kamigyō

    Tenjaku

    Michelin Bib Gourmand tempura-kaiseki house inherited from the chef's grandfather in Nishijin; its signature dresses tempura in chopped onion and mustard.

    570 Botanboko-chō, Kamigyō-ku, Kyoto 602-8475, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin Bib

  40. Worth the detour · Izakaya, Yakitori & Yokochō · Kita & Kamigyō

    Sambongi Shoten

    Michelin Bib Gourmand char-grill izakaya run by a former French chef — straw-smoked fish and venison and duck grilled as whole cuts.

    478 Shin-chō, Kamigyō-ku, Kyoto 602-0866, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin Bib

  41. Deep cut · Kita & Kamigyō

    Zuihō-in, Daitoku-ji (瑞峯院)

    Daitoku-ji sub-temple honouring Christian daimyō Ōtomo Sōrin; in the early 1960s Shigemori Mirei set the rear rock garden's stones in the shape of a cross.

    Murasakino Daitokuji-chō, Kita-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org), Lonely Planet, Inside Kyoto (Chris Rowthorn)

  42. Deep cut · Kita & Kamigyō

    Ōbai-in, Daitoku-ji (黄梅院)

    Daitoku-ji sub-temple founded 1562 with interlinked gardens — a rich moss garden and a stark kare-sansui; open to the public only in some seasons (notably autumn).

    Murasakino Daitokuji-chō, Kita-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org), Lonely Planet, Inside Kyoto (Chris Rowthorn)

  43. Deep cut · Kita & Kamigyō

    Rozan-ji

    Tendai temple on the site of Murasaki Shikibu's residence, east of the Imperial Palace, with a raked-gravel and moss 'Genji garden' of bellflowers.

    Kamigyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Wikipedia

  44. Deep cut · Kita & Kamigyō

    Kenkun Shrine & Funaoka-yama (建勲神社・船岡山)

    Shrine on Funaoka hill dedicated to the spirit of unifier Oda Nobunaga; the small hill park near Daitoku-ji gives views over the city.

    Funaoka-yama, Kita-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org), Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org), Matcha — Japan Travel Guide

  45. Deep cut · Kita & Kamigyō

    Ōta Shrine (大田神社), Kamigamo

    Small shrine near Kamigamo Shrine famous for its pond of irises, on a route through the old shrine-priest (shake) quarter.

    Kamigamo, Kita-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org), Kyoto City Tourism

  46. Deep cut · Kita & Kamigyō

    Nishijin Textile Center (西陣織会館)

    In the heart of the Nishijin weaving district: displays of fabrics and kimono, weaving demonstrations, a shop, and free short kimono fashion shows through the day.

    Nishijin, Kamigyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Lonely Planet, Inside Kyoto (Chris Rowthorn)

Rakusai 44

Ukyō & Nishikyō (Arashiyama · Sagano · Ryōan-ji · Katsura · Koke-dera

  1. Must see · Rakusai

    Togetsukyō Bridge

    Arashiyama's 'Moon-Crossing Bridge' over the Katsura River — a landmark since the Heian period, last rebuilt in the 1930s, framed by the forested Arashiyama hills.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Kyoto City Tourism, Wikipedia

  2. Must see · Rakusai

    Arashiyama Bamboo Grove

    The roughly 400-metre path through towering bamboo between Tenryū-ji's north gate and Nonomiya Shrine — go at dawn to beat the crowds.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Kyoto City Tourism, Wikipedia

  3. Must see · Tofu, Shōjin & Vegetarian · Rakusai

    Saga Tofu Morika (嵯峨豆腐 森嘉)

    A tofu maker dating from the Ansei era (1850s) whose soft, smooth Saga tofu shaped Kyoto's idea of tofu. It appears in Kawabata Yasunari's novel Koto, and Arashiyama yudofu restaurants use its tofu.

    Saga, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Walkerplus (kadokawa), Wa-raku / intojapanwaraku (Shogakukan), Mapple (Shobunsha)

  4. Must see · Rakusai

    Myōshin-ji

    Walled Rinzai Zen complex of about 50 sub-temples, head of a school of over 3,000 temples, founded in 1337 when a retired emperor gave his villa to Zen.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  5. Must see · Rakusai

    Katsura Imperial Villa

    The 17th-century princely villa often called the pinnacle of Japanese garden and architectural design — teahouses around a stroll-garden pond; Imperial Household Agency tours by reservation.

    Nishikyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Agency For Cultural Affairs, Wikipedia

  6. Must see · Rakusai

    Saihō-ji (Koke-dera, Moss Temple)

    The 'Moss Temple' — a garden carpeted with over a hundred kinds of moss; visits are by advance reservation only. UNESCO 688-011.

    Nishikyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO, Wikipedia

  7. Must see · Rakusai

    Tenryū-ji

    Head temple of the Rinzai Tenryū-ji school, founded 1339, with Musō Soseki's Sōgen pond garden borrowing the Arashiyama hills; UNESCO 688-012.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO, Wikipedia

  8. Must see · Rakusai

    Ryōan-ji

    Home of Japan's most famous dry rock garden — fifteen stones on raked gravel; UNESCO 688-015.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO, Wikipedia

  9. Must see · Wagashi, Matcha & Sweets · Rakusai

    Nakamuraken (中村軒)

    Long-established wagashi house facing Katsura Rikyū; red-bean paste still cooked the original way in a wood-fired okudo-san.

    Opposite Katsura Imperial Villa, Nishikyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Leaf Kyoto (京都リーフ)

  10. Must see · Kaiseki, Kyō-ryōri & Ryōtei · Rakusai

    Kitcho Arashiyama Honten (吉兆 嵐山本店)

    Kyoto's spare-no-expense kaiseki temple on the Arashiyama riverbank (Inside Kyoto: 'THE place to go').

    Arashiyama, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Inside Kyoto (Chris Rowthorn), Savor Japan

  11. Must see · Tofu, Shōjin & Vegetarian · Rakusai

    Ajiro Honten

    MICHELIN-listed shōjin ryōri at the south gate of Myōshin-ji; soy-flour udon is the signature.

    28-3 Hanazono Teranomaecho, Ukyo-ku, Kyoto, 616-8041, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin

  12. Must see · Tofu, Shōjin & Vegetarian · Rakusai

    Shigetsu

    Buddhist vegetarian temple cuisine served inside Tenryū-ji's World Heritage grounds (Michelin Bib Gourmand): sesame tofu, deep-fried tofu with vegetables, dressed greens.

    68 Saga-Tenryūji Susukinobaba-chō, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto 616-8385, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin Bib

  13. Must see · Soba & Udon · Rakusai

    Okina

    One MICHELIN Star (2026) soba house in Saga by Seiryō-ji (Saga Shakadō), Arashiyama.

    11 Saga-Shakadō Daimon-chō, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto 616-8422, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin ★

  14. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Yoshimine-dera (善峯寺)

    Tendai mountain temple in the western hills, founded 1029 by the priest Gensan; known for a 600-year-old pine only 2 m tall but 40 m wide.

    1372 Ōharano Oshio-chō, Nishikyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  15. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Jizō-in, the Bamboo Temple (地蔵院)

    Quiet 14th-century Rinzai Zen 'Bamboo Temple' among soaring stalks — the calm alternative to the Arashiyama grove.

    23 Yamada Kita-no-chō, Nishikyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Lonely Planet, Kyoto City Tourism, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  16. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Ōkōchi Sansō

    Silent-film star Ōkōchi Denjirō's hillside villa at the top of the bamboo grove — gardens, teahouses and a matcha with views over Kyoto.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  17. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Adashino Nenbutsu-ji

    Sagano temple holding some 8,000 stone Buddhas and statues for the souls of the dead, with its own small bamboo grove; candle-lit Sentō Kuyō in August.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  18. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Iwatayama Monkey Park

    A ten-minute hike up from just south of Togetsukyō to a hilltop where dozens of Japanese macaques roam freely, with a view over Kyoto.

    Nishikyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  19. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Otagi Nenbutsu-ji

    At the far end of Sagano, a temple of 1,200 moss-softened stone rakan statues, each carved by a different amateur sculptor with its own expression.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Wikipedia

  20. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Daikaku-ji

    Emperor Saga's 9th-century detached palace turned Shingon temple, beside the Ōsawa Pond — one of Japan's oldest surviving garden ponds and a moon-viewing spot.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Wikipedia

  21. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Nonomiya Shrine

    Small shrine in the bamboo grove with a rare black (unbarked) torii, where imperial princesses purified themselves before serving at Ise; appears in The Tale of Genji.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  22. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Matsunoo Taisha

    One of Kyoto's oldest shrines (701), patron of sake brewers — barrels donated by breweries line the grounds — with Shigemori Mirei's Shōwa-era gardens.

    Nishikyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Wikipedia

  23. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Kōryū-ji

    Founded in 603 by the Hata clan — Kyoto's oldest temple — whose Reihōden treasure hall holds the serene Miroku Bosatsu, Japan's first National Treasure sculpture.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Wikipedia

  24. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Toei Kyoto Studio Park

    Uzumasa film-set theme park — Edo-period streets still used to shoot samurai dramas, with ninja shows and costume photo studios.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  25. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Jōjakkō-ji

    Hillside temple on Mount Ogura above the bamboo grove — quiet most of the year, spectacular when its maples turn in autumn.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  26. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Nison-in

    Sagano temple named for its two Buddha statues, Shaka and Amida, approached up a long maple-lined avenue.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  27. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Giō-ji

    Tiny thatched nunnery in a luxuriant moss garden, named for the dancer Giō who retreated here after Taira no Kiyomori spurned her.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  28. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Seiryō-ji (Saga Shakadō)

    'Saga Shakadō', famed for its wooden Buddha statue and as a training centre of Yūzū nembutsu.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  29. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Ninna-ji

    Former imperial temple (founded 888) known for its late-blooming Omuro dwarf cherry trees and five-storey pagoda; UNESCO 688-007.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO, Wikipedia

  30. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Rakushisha (落柿舎), Sagano

    The thatched hut of the 17th-century haiku poet Mukai Kyorai, a disciple of Bashō, set among Sagano's fields. Small entry fee.

    Saga-Ogurayama, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  31. Worth the detour · Rakusai

    Saga-Toriimoto Preserved Street (嵯峨鳥居本)

    A Meiji-period street of preserved machiya at the far end of Sagano, below the torii of Atago Shrine. Many of the houses are now tea houses and shops. Free.

    Saga-Toriimoto, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  32. Worth the detour · Tofu, Shōjin & Vegetarian · Rakusai

    Yudōfu Sagano (湯豆腐 嵯峨野)

    Arashiyama's spacious, reliable yudofu house — the easy sit-down after the bamboo grove.

    Sagano / Arashiyama, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Lonely Planet, Kyoto City Tourism

  33. Worth the detour · Soba & Udon · Rakusai

    Arashiyama Yoshimura (嵐山よしむら)

    Soba in an old mansion overlooking the Katsura River and Togetsukyō — the classic Arashiyama lunch.

    Beside Togetsukyō Bridge, Saga, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Lonely Planet, Matcha — Japan Travel Guide

  34. Worth the detour · Tofu, Shōjin & Vegetarian · Rakusai

    Seizan Sōdō (西山艸堂), Tenryū-ji

    Yudofu served in a Tenryū-ji sub-temple, using smooth tofu from the Saga maker Morika. The menu is a single set.

    Saga-Tenryūji, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto (in a Tenryū-ji sub-temple)

    Recommended by Rurubu (JTB Publishing, rurubu.jp), Walkerplus (kadokawa)

  35. Worth the detour · Tofu, Shōjin & Vegetarian · Rakusai

    Ryōan-ji Seigen-in (龍安寺 西源院)

    A sub-temple restaurant inside UNESCO-listed Ryōan-ji, where every seat looks onto the garden. It is known for its seven-vegetable yudofu.

    Inside Ryōan-ji, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Rurubu (JTB Publishing, rurubu.jp), Walkerplus (kadokawa)

  36. Worth the detour · Teishoku, Curry & Yōshoku · Rakusai

    Unagi Hirokawa (うなぎ 廣川), Arashiyama

    An eel specialist on Arashiyama's main street, grilling over binchōtan charcoal. Expect queues or book ahead.

    44-1 Saga-Tenryūji Kitatsukurimichi-chō, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto (3 min walk from Randen Arashiyama Station)

    Recommended by Inside Kyoto (Chris Rowthorn), Leaf Kyoto (京都リーフ)

  37. Worth the detour · Tofu, Shōjin & Vegetarian · Rakusai

    Tōfu Ryōri Matsugae (豆腐料理 松ヶ枝), Arashiyama

    An Arashiyama tofu restaurant serving yudofu and yuba.

    Arashiyama, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Rurubu (JTB Publishing, rurubu.jp), byFood (byfood.com)

  38. Worth the detour · Tempura, Tonkatsu & Agemono · Rakusai

    Tempura Hashimoto

    Added by MICHELIN inspectors July 2026 — a tempura counter in Saga-Arashiyama near Tenryū-ji.

    23-9 Sagatenryuji Imahoricho, Ukyo-ku, Kyoto, 616-8366, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin

  39. Worth the detour · Ramen & Tsukemen · Rakusai

    Ramenya Fujitora

    New Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) ramen shop in Uzumasa, its bowls built on a chicken-and-pork broth.

    15-7 Uzumasa-Yasui Tsujinouchi-chō, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto 616-8076, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin Bib

  40. Deep cut · Rakusai

    Kameyama-kōen Park (亀山公園), Arashiyama

    A hilltop park at the top of the bamboo grove path, with a lookout over the Hozu gorge and fewer crowds. Free.

    Saga-Kamenoo-chō, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto (top of the Arashiyama bamboo grove path)

    Recommended by Lonely Planet, Inside Kyoto (Chris Rowthorn), Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  41. Deep cut · Rakusai

    Suzumushi-dera (Kegon-ji, 華厳寺)

    Kegon-ji, popularly 'Suzumushi-dera' (the bell-cricket temple), on the western hills near Koke-dera.

    31 Matsumuro Jike-chō, Nishikyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  42. Deep cut · Rakusai

    Hōrin-ji (法輪寺, Saga Kokūzō), Arashiyama

    'Saga Kokūzō' — the hillside temple on the Arashiyama side of Togetsukyō.

    68 Arashiyama Kokūzōyama-chō, Nishikyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  43. Deep cut · Rakusai

    Hōgon-in (宝厳院)

    Sub-temple of Tenryū-ji with a pleasant stroll garden and many monk statues by the entrance.

    Saga Tenryūji Susukinobaba-chō, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  44. Deep cut · Rakusai

    Umenomiya Taisha (梅宮大社)

    An ancient shrine to the gods of sake brewing and of childbirth, with a celebrated plum garden and a pond garden of irises and azaleas.

    Umezu, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Wikipedia, Kanpai (kanpai-japan.com)

Fushimi & Minami 34

Fushimi Inari · Tō-ji · Fushimi sake district · Daigo-ji

  1. Must see · Fushimi & Minami

    Fushimi Inari Taisha

    Head shrine of the thousands of Inari shrines across Japan, dedicated to the god of rice and sake by the Hata clan in the 8th century — tunnels of thousands of vermilion torii climb Mount Inari.

    Fushimi-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Kyoto City Tourism, Wikipedia

  2. Must see · Sushi & Kaisen-don · Fushimi & Minami

    Nezameya (祢ざめ家), Fushimi Inari

    A Fushimi Inari eatery open since 1540; the name is said to have come from Toyotomi Hideyoshi. Its inari-zushi is the shrine's own dish, and it also sells grilled sparrow and quail skewers to go.

    Fukakusa, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto (by the torii at the back approach to Fushimi Inari Taisha)

    Recommended by Good Luck Trip (gltjp.com), OnTrip Jal (Japan Airlines), Keihan Electric Railway — Kyoto navi

  3. Must see · Kaiseki, Kyō-ryōri & Ryōtei · Fushimi & Minami

    Uosaburō (魚三楼), Fushimi

    A Fushimi ryōtei founded in 1764. In the 1868 Battle of Toba-Fushimi the Shinsengumi and Satsuma troops fought in the street outside, and bullet holes are still in the lattice of the entrance.

    Kyōmachi 3-chōme, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Rurubu (JTB Publishing, rurubu.jp), Kyoto City Tourism, Savor Japan

  4. Must see · Fushimi & Minami

    Gekkeikan Okura Sake Museum

    Museum of Gekkeikan, one of Fushimi's largest and oldest brewers, in a renovated 1909 sake storehouse beside the Horikawa canal — traditional brewing tools and a tasting at the end.

    Fushimi-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Kyoto City Tourism

  5. Must see · Fushimi & Minami

    Tō-ji (Kyō-ō-gokoku-ji)

    Founded in 796 as the guardian temple at the old capital's south gate; its five-storey pagoda is Japan's tallest wooden pagoda, and a flea market fills the grounds on the 21st of each month. UNESCO 688-003.

    Minami-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO, Wikipedia

  6. Must see · Fushimi & Minami

    Daigo-ji

    Vast Shingon temple complex whose five-storey pagoda (951) is the oldest building in Kyoto; Toyotomi Hideyoshi's famous cherry-blossom party was held here. UNESCO 688-006.

    Fushimi-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO, Wikipedia

  7. Must see · Sake, Awamori, Whisky & Bars · Fushimi & Minami

    Kizakura Kappa Country (黄桜 カッパカントリー)

    Brewery restaurant of Kizakura, one of Fushimi's big houses — the one place to drink both its sake and its own craft beer.

    Fushimi Sake District, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Lonely Planet

  8. Must see · Sake, Awamori, Whisky & Bars · Fushimi & Minami

    Kyoto Brewing Company (京都醸造)

    Kyoto's flagship craft brewery, founded by an American, a Welshman and a Canadian; weekend tasting room at the brewery.

    Minami-ku, Kyoto (south of Kyoto Station)

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Lonely Planet

  9. Must see · Izakaya, Yakitori & Yokochō · Fushimi & Minami

    Torisei Honten (鳥せい 本店), Fushimi

    Opened 1976 by the 330-year-old Yamamoto Honke brewery inside an old sake storehouse: chicken built to go with its own sake.

    Fushimi Sake District, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto (in a converted Yamamoto Honke brewery building)

    Recommended by Leaf Kyoto (京都リーフ), Kyoto City Tourism

  10. Must see · International & Fusion · Fushimi & Minami

    anpeiji

    One MICHELIN Star in Fushimi — chef Masashi Anpeiji's sauce-led light French cooking.

    56 Nakajima Hinokamicho, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto, 612-8465, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin ★

  11. Worth the detour · Fushimi & Minami

    Bishamon-dō (毘沙門堂), Yamashina

    Tendai temple just over the Higashiyama hills in Yamashina, founded (per tradition) by the monk Gyōki in 703.

    18 Anshu Inariyama-chō, Yamashina-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Inside Kyoto (Chris Rowthorn), Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  12. Worth the detour · Fushimi & Minami

    Sanbō-in, Daigo-ji (醍醐寺 三宝院)

    Former head-priest residence of Daigo-ji, first built 1115; the present buildings and landscape garden date from 1598, when Toyotomi Hideyoshi rebuilt it for his Daigo cherry-blossom party — a Special Historic Site and Special Place of Scenic Beauty.

    Daigo, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org), Kyoto City Tourism, Japan-guide

  13. Worth the detour · Fushimi & Minami

    Kōbō-san Market at Tō-ji (弘法市)

    Huge flea market on Tō-ji's grounds on the 21st of every month, from early morning to about 16:30 — antiques, old kimono, crafts, plants and food from vendors across Japan.

    Tō-ji, Minami-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Japan-guide, Inside Kyoto (Chris Rowthorn)

  14. Worth the detour · Fushimi & Minami

    Teradaya Inn

    The Fushimi boat-inn where Sakamoto Ryōma was attacked by shogunate police in 1866; rebuilt after the 1868 Battle of Toba–Fushimi and open to visitors with Bakumatsu relics.

    Fushimi-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Kyoto City Tourism

  15. Worth the detour · Fushimi & Minami

    Jikkokubune Canal Cruise

    Replica Edo-period covered riverboats glide 50 minutes down the Horikawa canal past the wood-and-plaster walls of Fushimi's sake breweries (seasonal).

    Fushimi-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Kyoto City Tourism

  16. Worth the detour · Fushimi & Minami

    Zuishin-in

    Shingon temple in Ono (Yamashina) on the site of the Heian poet Ono no Komachi's residence — prayed at for romantic matches; its plum garden blooms in March.

    Yamashina-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Wikipedia

  17. Worth the detour · Fushimi & Minami

    Kajū-ji

    Head temple of the Shingon Yamashina school, an imperial-linked temple with a broad Heian-style pond garden.

    Yamashina-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Wikipedia

  18. Worth the detour · Fushimi & Minami

    Hōkai-ji (Hino Yakushi)

    Hino's Fujiwara-era temple whose Amida Hall and seated Amida statue are National Treasures.

    Fushimi-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Agency For Cultural Affairs, Wikipedia

  19. Worth the detour · Fushimi & Minami

    Jōnan-gū

    Shrine founded with the Heian capital in 794 to guard its south; famed for its gardens tracing Japanese garden history and its weeping plums.

    Fushimi-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  20. Worth the detour · Fushimi & Minami

    Fushimi Momoyama Mausoleum (Emperor Meiji)

    Emperor Meiji's tumulus on the old Fushimi Castle hill, reached by a long, wide stone stairway through the woods.

    Momoyama-chō Kojōyama, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  21. Worth the detour · Teishoku, Curry & Yōshoku · Fushimi & Minami

    Jukuseibuta Kawamura

    Michelin Bib Gourmand in Yamashina, east of Fushimi, specialising in aged pork sourced from a Fushimi butcher.

    57-1 Takehana Nishinoguchi-chō, Yamashina-ku, Kyoto 607-8089, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin Bib

  22. Deep cut · Fushimi & Minami

    Ōishi Shrine (大石神社), Yamashina

    A shrine founded in 1935 for Ōishi Kuranosuke, leader of the 47 rōnin of Akō, near where he lived in retreat in Yamashina. It is known for its autumn colours.

    116 Nishinoyama Sakurababa-chō, Yamashina-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org), Kyoto City Tourism, Keihan Electric Railway — Kyoto navi

  23. Deep cut · Fushimi & Minami

    Fushimi Castle

    Site of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's retirement castle on Momoyama hill, around which the Fushimi sake town grew; today's keep is a modern reconstruction.

    Fushimi-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  24. Deep cut · Fushimi & Minami

    Sekihō-ji

    Ōbaku temple just south of Fushimi Inari whose hillside holds hundreds of stone rakan designed by the painter Itō Jakuchū.

    26 Fukakusa Sekihōjiyama-chō, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  25. Deep cut · Fushimi & Minami

    Fujinomori Shrine

    Fukakusa shrine near Keihan Fujinomori Station, associated with horses and victory and known for its hydrangea garden.

    609 Fukakusa Toriizaki-chō, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  26. Deep cut · Fushimi & Minami

    Kanshū-ji (勧修寺), Yamashina

    Temple of the Yamashina valley founded in the early Heian period, after the capital moved to Heian-kyō.

    27-6 Kanshūji Niōdō-chō, Yamashina-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  27. Deep cut · Fushimi & Minami

    Gokō-no-miya Shrine (御香宮神社)

    Fushimi's shrine near the sake district; it holds its summer purification rite at the end of July, by the lunar calendar.

    174 Gokōnomiya Monzen-chō, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  28. Deep cut · Fushimi & Minami

    Chōken-ji (長建寺), Fushimi

    Red-walled temple to Benzaiten at the heart of the Fushimi sake district, with huge ginkgo trees — look for the 'Maria' figure on a lantern base.

    511 Higashiyanagi-chō, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  29. Deep cut · Fushimi & Minami

    Kyoto Racecourse (京都競馬場)

    JRA racecourse opened at this site in 1925 (capacity 120,000), home of the Kikuka Shō, the last leg of Japan's Triple Crown; reopened April 2023 after a grandstand rebuild.

    Fushimi-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org), Wikipedia

  30. Deep cut · Fushimi & Minami

    Rajōmon Gate Site (羅城門跡)

    Site of Heian-kyō's great southern gate (built 789) at the end of Suzaku Avenue; nothing survives but a stone pillar near Kujō and Senbon streets.

    Karahashi Rajōmon-chō, Minami-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org), Wikipedia

  31. Deep cut · Fushimi & Minami

    Fushimi Port Park (伏見港公園)

    Park on the filled-in site of the old Fushimi river port near Chūshojima, known for cherry blossoms, with a walking course, pools and lawns.

    Chūshojima, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org), Kyoto City Tourism

  32. Deep cut · Fushimi & Minami

    Mausoleum of Emperor Tenji (天智天皇山科陵 / 御廟野古墳)

    Octagonal kofun identified as the tomb of Emperor Tenji (38th emperor), venerated as his imperial mausoleum in Yamashina.

    Goryō, Yamashina-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org), Wikipedia

  33. Deep cut · Fushimi & Minami

    Nogi Shrine (乃木神社), Fushimi

    A shrine built in 1916 to General Nogi Maresuke and his wife. Its treasure hall holds more than 100 of the general's effects.

    32-2 Momoyama-chō Itakura Suō, Fushimi-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org), Kyoto City Tourism

  34. Deep cut · Fushimi & Minami

    Kisshōin Tenmangū (吉祥院天満宮)

    Said to be the first Tenmangū shrine to Sugawara no Michizane, founded in 934 by imperial order of Emperor Suzaku.

    3 Kisshōin Mandokoro-chō, Minami-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org), Kyoto City Tourism

Rakuhoku mountains 19

Ōhara · Kurama · Kibune · Takao · Miyama

  1. Must see · Markets, Depachika & Street Food · Rakuhoku mountains

    Doi Shibazuke Honpo, Ōhara Honten (土井志ば漬本舗 大原本店)

    The white-walled head shop of Ōhara's best-known shibazuke maker, where pickles are still fermented and aged naturally in the old way.

    41 Yase Hanajiri-chō, Sakyō-ku, Kyoto (Ōhara road)

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Rurubu (JTB Publishing, rurubu.jp), Kyoto Shimbun

  2. Must see · Rakuhoku mountains

    Sanzen-in

    Ōhara's great Tendai temple, its origins traced to the monk Saichō: moss gardens with small jizō statues under maples, at its finest in mid-November.

    Sakyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  3. Must see · Rakuhoku mountains

    Kurama-dera

    Mountain temple on Mount Kurama, legendary training ground of the young warrior Minamoto no Yoshitsune; a forest trail crosses the ridge down to Kibune.

    Sakyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Wikipedia

  4. Must see · Rakuhoku mountains

    Kifune Shrine

    Shrine to the god of water up the Kibune valley, its stone steps lined with red lanterns; summer visitors dine on kawadoko platforms over the river below.

    Sakyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Wikipedia

  5. Must see · Rakuhoku mountains

    Jingo-ji

    Shingon temple founded in 781, up a few hundred stone steps in the Takao maple valley — one of Kyoto's three classic autumn-leaf gorges; throw clay kawarake discs off the cliff for luck.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Wikipedia

  6. Must see · Rakuhoku mountains

    Miyama Kayabuki-no-Sato (Kitamura)

    Mountain village of nearly 40 thatched-roof farmhouses — the highest proportion of thatched houses anywhere in Japan; a preserved historic district.

    Miyama-chō, Nantan, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  7. Must see · Rakuhoku mountains

    Kōzan-ji

    Mountain temple in Toganoo above Takao, keeper of the Chōjū-giga animal scrolls often called Japan's first manga; UNESCO 688-010.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO, Wikipedia

  8. Must see · Kaiseki, Kyō-ryōri & Ryōtei · Rakuhoku mountains

    Miyamaso

    Mountain ryokan in Hanase promoted to Three MICHELIN Stars in 2026 — Kyoto's first new three-star in six years — for satoyama cuisine of chef-foraged wild vegetables, river fish, mushrooms and game.

    375 Hanase Harachi-chō, Sakyō-ku, Kyoto 601-1102, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin ★

  9. Worth the detour · Kaiseki, Kyō-ryōri & Ryōtei · Rakuhoku mountains

    Seryō (芹生), Ōhara

    A gasshō-style inn-restaurant beside Sanzen-in cooking Ōhara's seasonal mountain vegetables. Its teahouse serves yomogi warabi-mochi.

    22 Ōhara Shōrinin-chō, Sakyō-ku, Kyoto (by Sanzen-in)

    Recommended by Rurubu (JTB Publishing, rurubu.jp), Mapple (Shobunsha), Walkerplus (kadokawa)

  10. Worth the detour · Rakuhoku mountains

    Hōsen-in

    Small Ōhara temple near Sanzen-in, viewed 'like a picture frame' from the tatami room with matcha — its centrepiece is a carefully pruned 700-year-old pine.

    Sakyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  11. Worth the detour · Rakuhoku mountains

    Jakkō-in

    Ōhara nunnery founded around 600, where Empress Kenreimon-in retired after the fall of the Heike — a closing scene of The Tale of the Heike.

    Sakyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  12. Worth the detour · Rakuhoku mountains

    Rurikō-in

    Yase villa-temple open only in seasonal windows, famous for maples reflected in its polished black lacquer desk ('yuka-momiji').

    Sakyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  13. Worth the detour · Rakuhoku mountains

    Kurama Onsen

    The most accessible hot spring from Kyoto, with indoor and outdoor baths at the upper end of Kurama village; it reopened in November 2024 after closing during the pandemic.

    Sakyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  14. Worth the detour · Rakuhoku mountains

    Jissō-in (実相院), Iwakura

    Temple of Iwakura in Kyoto's northern hills, with gardens — a quiet detour on the way to Kurama.

    121 Iwakura Agura-chō, Sakyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Inside Kyoto (Chris Rowthorn), Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  15. Worth the detour · Kaiseki, Kyō-ryōri & Ryōtei · Rakuhoku mountains

    Kibune Hiroya (貴船 ひろや)

    Inn and restaurant founded in 1932 beside Kifune Shrine. It is one of Kibune's best-known kawadoko spots, serving meals on platforms over the river in summer and a momiji kaiseki out of season.

    Kibune-chō, Sakyō-ku, Kyoto (near Kifune Shrine)

    Recommended by Good Luck Trip (gltjp.com), Mapple (Shobunsha)

  16. Deep cut · Rakuhoku mountains

    Saimyō-ji (Makinoo)

    Small Shingon temple in Makinoo between Jingo-ji and Kōzan-ji, one of the 'three o' maple gorges of Takao.

    Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  17. Deep cut · Rakuhoku mountains

    Jikkō-in (実光院), Ōhara

    Small Ōhara temple just north of Sanzen-in, loved for its garden and fudan-zakura cherry that blooms October–March; tea and a sweet with entry.

    187 Ōhara Shōrinin-chō, Sakyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Lonely Planet, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  18. Deep cut · Rakuhoku mountains

    Shōrin-in (勝林院), Ōhara

    Ōhara's thatched-roof hall of shōmyō Buddhist chant, with a spectacular golden Amida statue.

    187 Ōhara Shōrinin-chō, Sakyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Lonely Planet, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  19. Deep cut · Rakuhoku mountains

    Raigō-in (来迎院), Ōhara

    Founded by Ennin in the 9th century and rebuilt in 1109 by Ryōnin as the seat of shōmyō chanting; a quiet climb above the Ōhara crowds.

    537 Ōhara Raigōin-chō, Sakyō-ku, Kyoto

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

Uji & Nara 43

Byōdō-in · Uji tea · Tōdai-ji · Kasuga Taisha · Nara Park

  1. Must see · Uji & Nara

    Hōryū-ji

    Founded in 607 by Prince Shōtoku; its pagoda and Golden Hall are the world's oldest surviving wooden buildings — Japan's first UNESCO World Heritage Site (Buddhist Monuments in the Hōryū-ji Area).

    Ikaruga, Ikoma District, Nara, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO, Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  2. Must see · Uji & Nara

    Nintendo Museum (ニンテンドーミュージアム)

    Nintendo's own museum, opened 2 Oct 2024 in the former Uji Ogura plant where it made hanafuda cards and repaired consoles — 135 years from playing cards to Switch, with hands-on exhibits.

    Your guide’s note ★ Anime & pop culture — Nintendo (Mario, Zelda, Pokémon) — the company's only museum, in its Kyoto home turf.

    Kaguraden-56, Ogura-chō, Uji, Kyoto Prefecture

    Recommended by Wikipedia, Official Site

  3. Must see · Uji & Nara

    Nara Park

    The large park at the heart of old Nara holding Tōdai-ji, Kasuga Taisha, Kōfuku-ji and the National Museum, roamed by more than a thousand free-ranging, bowing sika deer.

    Nara, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  4. Must see · Uji & Nara

    Byōdō-in

    The 11th-century Phoenix Hall pictured on the 10-yen coin, reflected in its Pure Land garden pond; UNESCO 688-008.

    Uji, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO, Wikipedia

  5. Must see · Wagashi, Matcha & Sweets · Uji & Nara

    Nakamura Tokichi Honten

    Uji tea merchant founded in 1859 on the Ujibashi-dōri shopping street; its café serves green-tea soba and matcha parfaits, with a tea room for grinding your own matcha.

    Ujibashi-dōri, Uji, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  6. Must see · Wagashi, Matcha & Sweets · Uji & Nara

    Itohkyuemon Uji Honten (伊藤久右衛門 宇治本店)

    Uji tea house founded in 1832; its main-store café is a matcha-parfait pilgrimage.

    Uji, Kyoto (main store)

    Recommended by Matcha — Japan Travel Guide, Savor Japan

  7. Must see · Kissaten & Coffee · Uji & Nara

    Tamaki-tei (たま木亭), Uji

    A bakery that draws bread fans from across Japan; owner-baker Jun Tamaki has taken top prizes at the Coupe du Monde de la Boulangerie. Closed Monday to Wednesday.

    57-14 Gokashō Hirano, Uji, Kyoto Prefecture

    Recommended by Leaf Kyoto (京都リーフ), Rurubu (JTB Publishing, rurubu.jp)

  8. Must see · Uji & Nara

    Tōdai-ji

    Nara's great temple, whose Daibutsuden houses the 15-metre bronze Great Buddha; UNESCO 'Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara' 870-001.

    Nara, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO

  9. Must see · Uji & Nara

    Kōfuku-ji

    Fujiwara clan temple whose five-storey pagoda rises over Nara Park, with a National Treasure Hall of Buddhist sculpture including the Ashura statue; UNESCO 870-002.

    Nara, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO

  10. Must see · Uji & Nara

    Kasuga Taisha

    Vermilion shrine of the Fujiwara famed for its thousands of stone and bronze lanterns, set against the protected Kasugayama Primeval Forest; UNESCO 870-003.

    Nara, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO

  11. Must see · Sushi & Kaisen-don · Uji & Nara

    Ike Edoyakiunagi Asahitei

    Bib Gourmand (2026) unagi house in Uda, Nara — father-to-son Edo-style grilling learned in Tokyo.

    29 Haibara Shimoidani, Uda, Nara, 633-0241, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin Bib

  12. Must see · International & Fusion · Uji & Nara

    Chugokusai Naramachi Kuko

    One MICHELIN Star Chinese in Naramachi — a garden-to-wok vegetable-led course.

    913-2 Kideracho, Nara, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin ★

  13. Must see · Okonomiyaki, Takoyaki & Kushikatsu · Uji & Nara

    Kushizukushi

    Michelin Bib Gourmand kushiage counter in Nara: creative seasonal fried skewers with Nara touches (sake-lees pickles, goma-dōfu), ending in nyūmen or dashi chazuke made with rice grown by the chef's brother.

    31 Yanagi-machi, Nara 630-8353, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin Bib

  14. Must see · Kaiseki, Kyō-ryōri & Ryōtei · Uji & Nara

    NARA NIKON

    Two MICHELIN Stars Japanese restaurant in Nara showcasing traditional cuisine shaped by the seasons.

    3 Nabeya-chō, Nara 630-8264, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin ★

  15. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Uji Bridge

    The main bridge over the Uji River, first built around 646 — one of Japan's oldest bridge sites — with Tsuen tea house at its east end.

    Your guide’s note ★ Anime & pop culture — Sound! Euphonium (Hibike! Euphonium, Kyoto Animation) — Uji, home of Kyoto Animation, is the series' real-life setting; the riverside bridges are anime-pilgrimage stops (Keihan's official Euphonium collaboration)

    Uji, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org), Anime News Network, Official Site

  16. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Daikichiyama Observation Deck (大吉山展望台, Buttoku-san)

    The lookout on Daikichiyama (officially Buttoku-san, 131.6 m) above the Uji river, with a view over all of Uji. It is a stamp point on the Keihan × Sound! Euphonium rally.

    Your guide’s note ★ Anime & pop culture — Sound! Euphonium (Kyoto Animation) — the observation deck where the protagonist and her friend play, in both the novel and the anime.

    Daikichiyama Fūchi Park, Uji, Kyoto Prefecture

    Recommended by Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org), Keihan Electric Railway — Kyoto navi, Walkerplus (kadokawa)

  17. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Mimuroto-ji

    Uji's 'flower temple' in the northern hills, founded some 1,200 years ago — vast gardens of azaleas, hydrangeas and lotuses in season.

    Uji, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  18. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Manpuku-ji

    Head temple of the Ōbaku school of Zen, founded by the Chinese monk Ingen in 1661 in Ming-dynasty Chinese style — and the home of fucha ryōri, Chinese-style vegetarian temple cuisine.

    Uji, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  19. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Nara National Museum

    National museum of Japanese Buddhist art in Nara Park; its autumn Shōsō-in exhibition of 8th-century imperial treasures is a national event.

    Nara, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  20. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Isui-en

    Two-part stroll garden (mid-17th century front, 1899 rear) that borrows Tōdai-ji's Nandaimon gate and Mount Wakakusa as scenery.

    Nara, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  21. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Mount Wakakusa

    The grass-covered hill behind Nara Park between Tōdai-ji and Kasuga Taisha, with open views over the city; its slopes are set alight each January in the Yamayaki.

    Nara, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  22. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Shin-Yakushi-ji

    Nara-period temple founded by an empress praying for the ailing emperor; the main hall rings the Yakushi Buddha with twelve clay guardian generals.

    Nara, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  23. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Nigatsu-dō

    Tōdai-ji's hillside hall with a free veranda view over Nara; stage of the Shuni-e (Omizutori) fire rite each March, held every year without a break for over 1,270 years.

    Nara, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  24. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Kōshō-ji (Uji)

    Sōtō Zen temple across the Uji River from Byōdō-in, approached up the maple-lined 'Kotozaka' slope.

    27 Uji-Yamada, Uji, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  25. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Tale of Genji Museum

    Uji city museum on The Tale of Genji, whose final 'Uji chapters' are set here — models, costumes and a film, with some English displays.

    45-26 Uji-Higashiuchi, Uji, Kyoto 611-0021, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  26. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Ujigami Shrine

    Small shrine across the Uji River from Byōdō-in whose main hall is regarded as Japan's oldest surviving shrine building; UNESCO 688-009.

    Uji, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO, Wikipedia

  27. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Kasugayama Primeval Forest (春日山原始林)

    Sacred forest on Mount Kasuga behind Kasuga Taisha — a component of the UNESCO 'Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara'.

    Kasugayama, Nara

    Recommended by UNESCO, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  28. Worth the detour · Wagashi, Matcha & Sweets · Uji & Nara

    Taihōan (対鳳庵), Uji

    Uji's public tea house: an authentic tea ceremony at a modest price, a short walk from Byōdō-in.

    Near Byōdō-in (by the Uji Tourist Information Center), Uji, Kyoto Prefecture

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Matcha — Japan Travel Guide

  29. Worth the detour · Wagashi, Matcha & Sweets · Uji & Nara

    Fukujuen Uji Kōbō (福寿園 宇治茶工房)

    Workshop of the 1790-founded Fukujuen tea house: grind your own matcha, then eat tea-based dishes upstairs.

    Across the Uji River from Taihōan, Uji, Kyoto Prefecture

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Matcha — Japan Travel Guide

  30. Worth the detour · Kaiseki, Kyō-ryōri & Ryōtei · Uji & Nara

    Kyō-Uji Matcha Ryōri Tatsumiya (辰巳屋), Uji

    Founded around 1840 as a tea merchant, this Uji house became a restaurant in 1912 and has cooked with Uji matcha for over a century.

    3-7 Uji Tamagawa, Uji, Kyoto Prefecture

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Savor Japan

  31. Worth the detour · Sushi & Kaisen-don · Uji & Nara

    Kakinoha-sushi Honpo Tanaka, Nara Honten (柿の葉すし本舗たなか なら本店)

    An old-established maker of kakinoha-zushi, Nara's persimmon-leaf sushi, sold from a single piece. It has an in-store tea room, Kakinoha Chaya.

    Nara city, Nara Prefecture

    Recommended by Narashikanko, Mapple (Shobunsha)

  32. Worth the detour · Wagashi, Matcha & Sweets · Uji & Nara

    Yoshino Honkuzu Tenkyokudō Nara Honten (吉野本葛 天極堂 奈良本店)

    A 150-year-old refiner of Yoshino kuzu starch, which still uses the traditional Yoshino-zarashi bleaching method. Its Nara shop makes kuzu sweets and kuzu dishes to order.

    Nara city (on the site of Tōdai-ji's former West Gate), Nara Prefecture

    Recommended by Mapple (Shobunsha), Wa-raku / intojapanwaraku (Shogakukan)

  33. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Gangō-ji

    Successor to Asuka-dera, Japan's first full-scale Buddhist temple; some roof tiles date to the 6th century. In the Naramachi old town. UNESCO 870-004.

    Nara, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO

  34. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Yakushi-ji

    Seventh-century imperial temple in western Nara whose East Pagoda is one of Japan's oldest; UNESCO 870-005.

    Nara, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO

  35. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Tōshōdai-ji

    Founded in 759 by the Chinese monk Ganjin (Jianzhen); its Golden Hall is the finest surviving Nara-period main hall. UNESCO 870-006.

    Nara, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO

  36. Worth the detour · Uji & Nara

    Heijō Palace Site

    The excavated site of the 8th-century imperial palace of Heijō-kyō, with the reconstructed Daigokuden and Suzakumon gate; UNESCO 870-007 (coordinate = centre of a 129 ha site).

    Nara, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO

  37. Worth the detour · Soba & Udon · Uji & Nara

    Gen

    MICHELIN-listed soba shop on a Naramachi sake brewery's premises, using the brewery's water.

    23-2 Fukuchiincho, Nara, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin

  38. Worth the detour · Soba & Udon · Uji & Nara

    Kiminami

    Michelin Bib Gourmand soba restaurant in north-western Nara city.

    2201-1 Oshikuma-chō, Nara 631-0011, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin Bib

  39. Worth the detour · International & Fusion · Uji & Nara

    toi Inshokuten

    Michelin Bib Gourmand (2026) Indian kitchen in Nara — 'toi' = 'trip of imagination' — serving meat, fish and vegetable curries thali-style as a teishoku.

    30-3 Hanashiba-chō, Nara 630-8266, Japan

    Recommended by Michelin Bib

  40. Deep cut · Uji & Nara

    Yoshiki-en

    Nara garden of moss, pond and tea-ceremony sections beside Isui-en, on the site of a Kōfuku-ji sub-temple.

    Nara, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  41. Deep cut · Uji & Nara

    Saidai-ji (西大寺), Nara

    The 'Great Western Temple', once one of Nara's seven great temples and counterpart to Tōdai-ji; Shakyamuni in the main hall and a fierce Aizen Myō-ō (spring and autumn viewings).

    1-1-5 Saidaiji Shiba-machi, Nara

    Recommended by Official Nara Travel Guide (visitnara.jp), Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  42. Deep cut · Uji & Nara

    Uji Shrine (宇治神社)

    Nagare-zukuri shrine 100 m below Ujigami Shrine — the two were one 'lower and upper shrine' until separated in the Meiji period.

    1 Uji Yamada, Uji, Kyoto Prefecture

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  43. Deep cut · Uji & Nara

    Agata Shrine (縣神社), Uji

    Shrine by Byōdō-in's south entrance, ten minutes' walk from Uji Station.

    72 Uji Renge, Uji, Kyoto Prefecture

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa 17

Amanohashidate · Ine no Funaya · Kameoka · Ōtsu · Hiei-zan

  1. Must see · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Amanohashidate

    The 3 km pine-covered sandbar across Miyazu Bay, one of the 'Three Views of Japan' — viewed upside-down through your legs (matanozoki) from the hilltop parks at either end.

    Miyazu, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  2. Must see · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Ine no Funaya (Ine boathouses)

    Fishing village of funaya — wooden boathouses with living quarters above, built right over the water around Ine Bay; best seen from a bay cruise.

    Ine, Yosa District, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  3. Must see · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Ishiyama-dera

    Shingon temple on wollastonite rocks above the Seta River, where Murasaki Shikibu is said to have begun The Tale of Genji; its main hall and Tahōtō pagoda are National Treasures.

    Ōtsu, Shiga, Japan

    Recommended by Agency For Cultural Affairs, Wikipedia

  4. Must see · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Mii-dera (Onjō-ji)

    Head temple of the Tendai Jimon school at the foot of Mount Hiei above Lake Biwa; its Kondō is a National Treasure and its evening bell one of the Eight Views of Ōmi.

    Ōtsu, Shiga, Japan

    Recommended by Agency For Cultural Affairs, Wikipedia

  5. Must see · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Hozugawa River Cruise (Hozu Gorge)

    Descent of the Hozu Gorge from Kameoka to Arashiyama in flat-bottomed boats steered by boatmen with oars and bamboo poles — often paired with the Sagano Scenic Railway.

    Kameoka – Arashiyama, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  6. Must see · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Enryaku-ji (Mount Hiei)

    Head temple of Tendai Buddhism, founded on Mount Hiei in 788 and spread across the forested summit above Lake Biwa; UNESCO 688-005 (coordinate is the property centre of a 498 ha precinct).

    Ōtsu, Shiga, Japan

    Recommended by UNESCO, Wikipedia

  7. Must see · Sake, Awamori, Whisky & Bars · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Mukai Shuzō (向井酒造), Ine

    Founded 1754 — 'the sake brewery closest to the sea in Japan', facing the Ine funaya boathouses.

    Ine Bay (by the funaya), Ine-chō, Yosa-gun, Kyoto Prefecture

    Recommended by Matcha — Japan Travel Guide, Time Out

  8. Worth the detour · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Chion-ji (智恩寺), Amanohashidate

    Rinzai Zen temple at the sandbar's southern entrance housing one of Japan's 'Three Important Monju Bosatsu' statues — students pray here for wisdom; 1500s two-storey tahōtō pagoda.

    Monju, Miyazu, Kyoto Prefecture (south end of the Amanohashidate sandbar)

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Amanohashidate, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  9. Worth the detour · Wagashi, Matcha & Sweets · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Kanō Shōjuan Sunainosato (叶 匠壽庵 寿長生の郷), Ōtsu

    The Ōmi confectioner's satoyama estate, where the head office moved 40 years ago. It has orchards, a restaurant, a bakery-café and hands-on wagashi making.

    4-2-1 Ōishi Ryūmon, Ōtsu, Shiga Prefecture

    Recommended by Biwako Visitors Bureau (biwako-visitors.jp), Wa-raku / intojapanwaraku (Shogakukan), Mapple (Shobunsha)

  10. Worth the detour · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Hiyoshi Taisha

    Head shrine of the Hie/Hiyoshi shrines, guardian of Enryaku-ji in the Sakamoto foothills of Mount Hiei; its East and West main halls are National Treasures and the grounds famous for autumn maples.

    Sakamoto, Ōtsu, Shiga, Japan

    Recommended by Agency For Cultural Affairs, Wikipedia

  11. Worth the detour · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Nariai-ji

    Saigoku pilgrimage temple in the hills on the north side of Amanohashidate, with a celebrated lookout over the sandbar.

    Miyazu, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  12. Worth the detour · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Kono Shrine (Moto-Ise)

    Ancient shrine at the north end of Amanohashidate, called 'Moto-Ise' for its link to the Grand Shrine of Ise.

    Miyazu, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Wikipedia

  13. Worth the detour · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Jōruri-ji

    Heian-period Pure Land temple in rural southern Kyoto Prefecture: nine Amida statues in a long hall facing a three-storey pagoda across a pond — both National Treasures.

    Kizugawa, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Agency For Cultural Affairs, Wikipedia

  14. Worth the detour · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Kasamatsu Park

    Hillside park above Kono Shrine, reached by chairlift or cable car, from where Amanohashidate is said to look like the kanji for 'one' — the classic upside-down matanozoki viewpoint.

    Miyazu, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Japan-guide, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  15. Deep cut · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Moto-Ise Naikū Kōtai Jinja (元伊勢内宮皇大神社)

    Said to have held Amaterasu's sacred mirror before it settled at Ise Jingū; keeps a tradition of prayers to repel oni.

    Fukuchiyama, Kyoto Prefecture

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, JNTO, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

  16. Deep cut · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Kaijūsen-ji

    Mountain temple in Kamo, Kizugawa, whose small Kamakura-period five-storey pagoda is a National Treasure.

    Kizugawa, Kyoto, Japan

    Recommended by Agency For Cultural Affairs, Wikipedia

  17. Deep cut · Kyoto Prefecture & Lake Biwa

    Fukuchiyama Castle (福知山城)

    Castle of the town Akechi Mitsuhide built while ruling the Tanba region under Oda Nobunaga.

    Fukuchiyama, Kyoto Prefecture

    Recommended by Kyoto City Tourism, Japanese Wikipedia (ja.wikipedia.org)

215 sights and 183 places to eat across Kyoto and its day-trip ring, every one traceable to its source: the seventeen UNESCO Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto and Nara's World Heritage temples, Gion and Pontochō, Arashiyama and Ōhara, Michelin-starred kaiseki and Bib Gourmand soba, saba-zushi and eel, Uji tea and the Fushimi sake district.

How this guide was made

How the cuisine filters were policed

Every food card names a specific dish — a label alone doesn’t qualify. A cuisine tag names the kitchen’s own tradition, never one dish it serves. Tabelog and Retty scores may measure popularity but never count as a source.

Web-searched in Japanese and English, fact-checked

Every place is traceable to two credible sources, or a lone Michelin / UNESCO / Agency for Cultural Affairs designation — recorded in data/sources.json. Every coordinate is verified into data/geocodes.json and every place status-checked open. Yelp/TripAdvisor/Tabelog never count toward the two-source bar.
